title: Do health and wellbeing measures agree?
text:
In progress. Data access being arranged through the UK Data Service.



Health and wellbeing outcome measures are used to compare treatments and to inform how health budgets are allocated. Several established instruments exist, and they do not always agree with each other about the same person. Where mapping functions convert between them, those functions are usually estimated on one survey sample and then applied elsewhere.
This project uses the SIPHER-HWMIC survey, which asked over 12,000 UK adults the questions from eight different health and wellbeing instruments, across three separate survey panels.
What the project will involve:

comparing scores from several preference-based instruments for the same respondents
testing whether mapping between instruments holds when trained on one survey panel and applied to another
reporting calibration as well as fit, the external-validation approach standard in clinical prediction modelling but uncommon in this literature
examining whether disagreement between instruments varies systematically by age, sex, socioeconomic position or health status
handling documented data quality problems in the survey and reporting to the MAPS statement, the mapping literature’s own reporting standard

title: Charlie McDermott
text:
I’m a health-focused data scientist with hands-on healthcare systems experience and an MSc in Computer Science with AI, focused on turning messy clinical data into equitable models and evidence. I write my analyses as reproducible pipelines in line with the NHS Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAP) approach and publish the code.
Before moving into data science I spent eight years at the University of Oxford’s simulation training and research centre at the John Radcliffe Hospital (NHS FT), building the data systems and technology behind clinical training. I have run an independent digital consultancy since 2012.
My MSc thesis used accelerometry data from the Millennium Cohort Study to examine how the duration and temporal structure of activity recordings affect ADHD prediction, comparing interpretable and complex models and testing for bias across subgroups. See Projects.

title: Taming ‘biggish’ data
text:
Clinical simulation training generates awkward data: courses, faculty, candidates, equipment, feedback and outcomes, all related and all changing. At OxSTaR, the University of Oxford’s simulation centre at the John Radcliffe Hospital, delivery was largely for NHS staff, and reporting went to NHS stakeholders, where it was used to account for how training spend translated into activity. I designed, built and maintained the MS Access database behind that reporting.
This project revisits that database design, rebuilt from scratch in T-SQL on SQL Server. The rebuild demonstrates the data model and the reporting rather than reproducing the original system: a schema built around NHS Data Dictionary code lists, business rules enforced by the database itself rather than the forms in front of it, a write path of stored procedures, and reporting views for the questions a centre’s leads ask. The trust, its people and all of the data are synthetic, and no code or data from the original system is used.
flowchart LR
    SG[staff_group] --> JR[job_role]
    JR --> P[person]
    ORG[organisation] --> DIV[division] --> SU[service_unit]
    ORG --> P
    SU -.-> P
    C[course] --> S[session]
    P --> SP[session_participant]
    S --> SP
    SP --> F[feedback]
    SP --> R[rpt views<br/>and procedures]
Arrows run from parent to child table; the dotted arrow is optional, as partner staff have no unit.
The design document sets out every table, rule and report in full; this page covers the highlights.

title: Taming ‘biggish’ data
text:
1. From requirements to rules

The centre’s leads described what they needed in plain terms: know who attended and who didn’t, never overbook a course, report staff in the role they held at the time, and use national codes so the numbers mean the same thing everywhere. Each requirement was translated into a rule and enforced at the lowest layer of the database able to hold it: column types and NOT NULL first, then keys, then CHECK constraints, with a trigger and stored procedures reserved for rules that depend on other rows or tables.









The centre needs
Rule
Enforced by




job roles recorded in national terms
job roles use NHS Data Dictionary codes, each within its staff group
foreign keys to the code lists, and a CHECK on the code


cancellations explained
a cancelled session carries a reason
CHECK constraint


one person leading each session
one lead faculty per session
filtered unique index

feedback only from attendees
composite foreign key through a persisted computed column


no course overbooked
no booking over capacity or onto a cancelled session
stored procedure, with a trigger as backstop

the booking procedure copies the role onto the booking



Each layer rejects a bad row with an error that names what was broken. The script behind this screenshot tries to break five rules, one per layer, inside transactions that are rolled back:



Five rules broken, five errors: a CHECK constraint (547), a filtered unique index (2601), a foreign key (547), the booking procedure (50010) and the trigger backstop (50010)


Rules summary:

16 rules in all, listed in the design with the error each one raises
every constraint is named for what it enforces (ck_, fk_, ux_ and so on), so an error message names the rule that was broken
built-in error numbers (547, 2601, 2627) and custom ones (50001 to 50021) give a front end fixed codes to map to friendly messages
rules that depend on another table, such as host-trust staff needing a service unit, sit in the procedures that write the data

title: Taming ‘biggish’ data
text:
2. Schema design

Three schemas separate the code lists (ref), the operational tables (core) and the reporting layer (rpt). Staff groups and job roles use the national codes from the NHS Data Model and Dictionary, loaded with their source and retrieval date, so a staff group in a report means what it means nationally. Keys do more than identify rows: composite foreign keys keep related records inside the same organisation, and filtered unique indexes express rules that only apply to some rows.

The booking table uses both. The unit copied onto a booking must belong to the organisation copied with it, and only the lead’s row must be unique per session:


206_core_session_participant.sql

CREATE TABLE core.session_participant
(
    -- ...
    CONSTRAINT fk_session_participant_service_unit FOREIGN KEY (organisation_id, service_unit_id)
        REFERENCES core.service_unit (organisation_id, service_unit_id)
        ON DELETE NO ACTION
);

CREATE UNIQUE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ux_session_participant_session_id_lead
    ON core.session_participant (session_id)
    WHERE role_code = 'LEAD';







Object Explorer: keys, constraints, indexes and the trigger on the booking table, each named for what it enforces








Schema summary:

10 staff groups and the 34 job roles in use, from the NHS Data Dictionary; a CHECK ties each job role code to its staff group through its first two characters
composite foreign keys stop a person or booking pointing at a unit in another organisation; the UNIQUE keys that look redundant are there as their targets
filtered unique indexes handle conditional uniqueness: one host trust, one lead per session, and email unique only when it’s given
every foreign key is indexed on the child side, which SQL Server doesn’t do automatically, and none cascade, so deleting a parent can’t erase history

title: Taming ‘biggish’ data
text:
3. The write path

Every write is designed to go through a stored procedure. Each runs in a transaction with XACT_ABORT ON and TRY/CATCH, so any error rolls back all of its work and reaches the caller with its original number. Booking is the most demanding case: two people booking the last place at the same moment must not both succeed, and the booking has to record the person’s role as it stands that day.

The booking procedure locks the session row before counting places, so concurrent bookings for the same session wait their turn rather than race:


305_core_usp_book_participant.sql

SELECT @status_code = s.status_code,
       @capacity    = s.capacity
FROM core.session AS s WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK)
WHERE s.session_id = @session_id;

IF @status_code = 'X'
    THROW 50011, N'The session is cancelled.', 1;

IF @role_code = 'DEL'
BEGIN
    SELECT @booked = COUNT(*)
    FROM core.session_participant AS sp
    WHERE sp.session_id = @session_id
      AND sp.role_code = 'DEL'
      AND sp.outcome_code <> 'X';

    IF @booked >= @capacity
        THROW 50010, N'The session is full.', 1;
END;

The same procedure copies the person’s organisation, job role and unit onto the booking, so when someone is promoted, their earlier bookings keep the role they held at the time:



One person either side of a promotion: each booking keeps the job role held when it was made


Write path summary:

seven procedures cover every write: adding a person, changing their role, creating, cancelling and booking sessions, recording attendance and adding feedback
UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK on the session row makes bookings for the same session queue, so two can’t both take the last place
a trigger repeats the capacity check as a backstop for any write that bypasses the procedure
copying the role at booking gives point-in-time reporting from a single table

title: Taming ‘biggish’ data
text:
4. Reporting

The reporting layer gives analysts a stable set of views over the operational tables, with the definitions written into the views rather than left to each query: rates count delegates only, cancelled places are excluded, the DNA rate is did-not-attend over attended plus did-not-attend, and dates map to NHS financial years and quarters through a date table. Staff groups come from the booking, so a report on last year shows staff as they were last year.

DNA rates by staff group and financial quarter come from a CTE that does the counting and a window function that compares each quarter with the one before:


530_rpt_v_dna_by_staff_group.sql

SELECT
    fy_quarter_label,
    staff_group_code,
    staff_group,
    delegates_due,
    dnas,
    CAST(dna_rate AS decimal(5, 1)) AS dna_rate_pct,
    -- LAG reads the same staff group's previous quarter; it is empty for the first one.
    CAST(dna_rate - LAG(dna_rate) OVER (PARTITION BY staff_group_code ORDER BY fy_label, fy_quarter)
         AS decimal(5, 1)) AS dna_rate_change_pts
FROM quarterly;




DNA rate by staff group, summed from the view across all quarters. Staff group 03’s higher rate is seeded into the synthetic data to exercise the report; it is not a finding.





Session register: GROUP BY ROLLUP adds a subtotal for each staff group and a total for the session





Faculty teaching load in 2025/26, ranked with RANK so equal counts share a place


Reporting summary:

rpt.v_participation is the base view: one row per booking, with course, organisation, division and the staff group held at the time
session fill and DNA rates, DNA trends by staff group and quarter, faculty load and the session register, built with CTEs, conditional aggregation, NULLIF against divide-by-zero, LAG, RANK and GROUP BY ROLLUP
a name search matches the start of a name with LIKE and similar-sounding surnames with SOUNDEX
rpt.dim_date maps every day from April 2022 to March 2027 to its NHS financial year and quarter

5. Build and documentation

The database is built entirely from code. One command drops and recreates it from master, runs the SQL files in numbered order, loads the national code lists and the calendar, then generates the synthetic data, so anyone with SQL Server can rebuild the same database.



python scripts/build.py

Build summary:

one object per file, numbered in build order, with every constraint named
national code lists stored as CSV with their source and retrieval date; NHS England content is excluded from the code’s MIT licence
synthetic data from a fixed seed: 2,200 staff across seven organisations and 650 sessions of 40 courses, April 2023 to December 2026, inserted through the same constraints and trigger as any other write
two patterns are seeded to exercise the reports: a higher DNA rate in staff group 03, and about 5% of staff changing role part-way through
every table and column carries a description, from which scripts/data_dictionary.py generates the data dictionary
the queries behind each screenshot are in the repo

title: Actigraphy and ADHD prediction
text:
Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) prediction has the potential to unlock solutions to the UK’s under-diagnosis crisis, realising health benefits and social opportunities for those stuck on waiting lists. A gap exists to test whether biomarkers from activity data — intra-daily and weekly temporal factors — can predict ADHD beyond the small convenience samples and opaque modelling approaches currently limiting transition of prediction technologies into clinical practice. This study addresses these limitations with interpretable, fair modelling on large-cohort MCS data, and reports on optimal activity monitoring durations, key for real-world application.
Built against the NHS RAP maturity framework: Baseline, with most of Silver in place. See Code README for full criteria.
flowchart LR
    A[MCS survey files<br/>4 sweeps] --> C[Labels, covariates,<br/>exclusions]
    B[Raw accelerometer<br/>.dat files] --> D[Non-wear flagging,<br/>day alignment]
    D --> E[tsfresh features<br/>per valid day]
    C --> F[Feature selection]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Model comparison,<br/>tuning]
    G --> H[Evaluation, subgroups,<br/>monitoring duration]
The analysis described below is the thesis as submitted, tagged v1.0.0. Version 2 at the end describes subsequent improvements to the pipeline as part of iterative, on-going code review.

title: Actigraphy and ADHD prediction
text:
1. Data extraction

Secondary data is sourced from the MCS via the UK Data Service. The MCS conducts longitudinal research on 18,827 children born around the millennium, collecting sweeps of observations, questionnaire and interview data every 2-3 years. Natural-setting activity data was collected for 7 days at age-7 with a waist-worn, non-invasive GT1M actigraph.

Survey data came as Stata files, differences between how Stata and pandas handle category naming required parsing:


extract.py

def drop_bad_cats(path, bad_cols):
    """Parse .stata data into pandas.

    Stata allows duplicate categorical labels, pandas throws an error. This
    function drops the offending columns, extracts cat labels and reapplys
    them in pandas.
    """
    with pd.io.stata.StataReader(path) as reader:
        df = reader.read(convert_categoricals=False)
        value_labels = reader.value_labels()

    df = df.drop(columns=bad_cols, errors="ignore")

    for col, labels in value_labels.items():
        if col not in df.columns or col in bad_cols:
            continue

        # skip columns whose labels are not unique
        if len(set(labels.values())) != len(labels.values()):
            continue

        df[col] = pd.Categorical(df[col].map(labels).fillna(df[col]))

    return df

Extraction summary:

class labels operationliased from any ADHD diagnosis reported across the four sweeps (ages 5, 7, 11, 14)
covariates joined from four more files, each with its own ID scheme
exclusions for confounders: autism, limited fitness, ADHD medication started before activity measurements
171.6 million 15-second epochs from raw .dat files, processed in chunks on a 40GB machine; tsfresh extraction ran around 15 hours
the whole pipeline reruns from source with two commands

title: Actigraphy and ADHD prediction
text:
2. Preprocessing algorithms

The raw timeseries data provides counts every 15 seconds and therefore appropriate for far more granular analysis of within-day features. However, in order to process this data it needed to be mapped to the valid and reliable sample first, this required development of two algorithms. The first applied a non-wear marker to each participant’s timeseries data, based on the same rules used by MCS to remain consistent. The second determined how many days offset the timeseries were from the first recorded valid day.

Non-wear is defined as 80 or more consecutive zero-count epochs. Finding every such run across millions of rows would be costly using loops, a vectorised algorithm was desinged instead:


timeseries.py

# flag for non-wear time: >=80 consecutive 0s
s = df.iloc[:, 0].eq(0)                              # boolean for zero count
groups = s.ne(s.shift()).cumsum()                    # groups for consec. true/false runs
run_lengths = s.groupby(groups).transform('size')    # broadcast run length back to rows
df["NW_flag"] = (s & (run_lengths >= NON_WEAR_RUN))  # flag rows 80+ zero-run

Preprocessing summary:

tabular data - survey responses and activity aggregates used to engineer handcrafted features - were cleaned, merged and processed into a valid sample based on inclusion and exclusion criteria
the offset algorithm aligns the timeseries data to the valid sample by sliding a day-length window along the recording until window wear-time statistics match the MCS record for the first valid day
where it could not match (0.2% of recordings), the participant was dropped. The effect of excluded data were analysed for sample bias by monitoring changes to class and covariate distributions

title: Actigraphy and ADHD prediction
text:
3. Feature selection

The large generic output of tsfresh is then subjected to a series of feature reduction methods to mitigate known problems for high-dimensional datasets. Features are then selected for consistently ranking well across a range of methods based on mutual information, f-scoring, regularised logistic regressors and extra trees. This range prevents any particular method dominating and applies broad assessment of feature importance.



selection.py

# feature consensus across selection methods
selected_sets = {
    name: set(vals)
    for name, vals in selected_features.items()
}

all_selected = sorted(set().union(*selected_sets.values()))

selection_matrix = pd.DataFrame({
    name: [feature in selected_sets[name] for feature in all_selected]
    for name in selected_sets
}, index=all_selected)

selection_matrix["n_methods"] = selection_matrix.sum(axis=1)


The most selected features by far are frequency and spectral-based such as Fourier derivations which reflect periods, oscillations and rhythms. Interestingly, the least prominent selected include the simpler sum/magnitude features most closely related to the handcrafted features.

1,554 candidate features to 442, keeping only those at least two methods agreed on
selection matrix doubles as an audit trail: which method kept what
interpretability: grouping 442 coefficients into families provides relevant clinical insights
weekday and weekend features are selected with equal importance (222 and 220), evidencing RQ2

title: Actigraphy and ADHD prediction
text:
4. Evaluation






ROC curve







Precision-recall curve






Logistic Regression consistently outperformed Naïve Bayes and Extra Trees in all conditions with the selected tsfresh-stratified features and across all metrics. Final scoring achieved AUROC 0.846 and AUPRC 5.9x baseline. Note the low precision scores reflecting high false positives, information that is absent from ROC analysis alone.




Participants ranked by predicted probability


Evaluation summary:

AUROC alone provides a threshold-agnostic score of how well the model ranks class, secondary metrics include AUPRC able to account for low class prevalence (1.8%) by revealing low precision scores
threshold analysis reveals the sensitivity/specificity trade-off:

the screening case: optimise for sensitivity, maximise true positives e.g. to send families on waiting lists information and support, where a false positive costs little
the diagnostic case: optmise for specificity, minimise false positives e.g. to diagnose and start treatment, where a false positive is costly

5. Subgroups and calibration

Algorithmic bias defines systematic errors due to biases in data, labels or modelling; even interpretable approaches are susceptible where healthy performance metrics on the whole dataset may belie performance discriminations between subgroups, potentially compounding existing inequalities.

The analysis reveals broadly comparable subgroup performance, with imbalance seen in higher female ranking metrics but also unstable due to prevalence. The model’s probabilities are substantially under-scaled and thus do not represent actual risk.

Subgroup summary:

ethnicity could not be analysed: 10 > non-white positive cases, despite MCS oversampling
the model ranks well, however this analysis reveals miscalibrated probabilities at the individual level, prompting recalibration methods as future work
analysing subgroups responds to the TRIPOD+AI framework for transparent and fair data processing and reporting

title: Actigraphy and ADHD prediction
text:
6. Significance tests guiding recommendations

To compare monitoring period durations, participants with at least six valid days monitoring were selected. Differences in AUROC and AUPRC between each reduced duration and the 6-day reference condition were assessed using paired bootstrap resampling, appropriate for non-independent samples.



evaluate.py

# paired bootstrap
boot_rows = []
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
duration_cols = {2: "probs_2", 3: "probs_3", 4: "probs_4", 5: "probs_5", 6: "probs_6"}

for _ in range(n_boot):
    sample = preds.iloc[rng.integers(0, len(preds), len(preds))]

    if sample["y"].nunique() < 2:
        continue

    for days, col in duration_cols.items():
        boot_rows.append({"days": days, **metrics(sample, col)})




AUROC by monitoring duration



Performance improved monotonically across AUROC, AUPRC and Spearman metrics as duration increased. 2- and 3-day durations were both substantially lower than the 6-day reference, found to be significant with p-values < 0.001. 5 days produced near-equivalent performance and was found to not be significantly different.

Conclusions:

Holm adjusted p-values on bootstrap resampling show significantly worse prediction power for 2 and 3 day monitoring durations, recommending at least 5 days of activity monitoring for reliable AUROC
using these techniques, observed patient data produced real-world recommendations for monitoring periods and data collection protocols, with implications for planning costs and minimising wear-time for children who may have sensitivities/wear-compliance issues
In addition, further research into ADHD actigraphy can realise weekday/weekend and intra-daily differences found to be important in differentiating the condition, and apply fair and interpretable methods to acheive this

title: Actigraphy and ADHD prediction
text:
Version 2: iterative improvement

After submission I reviewed the pipeline and made changes below, released as v2.0.0. The full difference is readable side by side.
Consensus selection within cross-validation folds


selection.py

class ConsensusSelector(SelectorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """Second pass consensus as a transformer, fitted on training folds only."""

    def __init__(self, selectors, n_consensus=N_CONSENSUS):
        self.selectors = selectors
        self.n_consensus = n_consensus

    def fit(self, X, y):
        votes = np.zeros(X.shape[1], dtype=int)

        for selector in self.selectors.values():
            votes += clone(selector).fit(X, y).get_support().astype(int)

        self.votes_ = votes
        self.support_ = votes >= self.n_consensus
        self.n_features_in_ = X.shape[1]
        return self

    def _get_support_mask(self):
        return self.support_

Updates:

consensus feature selection now runs inside each training fold, wrapped in a scikit-learn transformer, reducing the potential for leakage from held-out data and following the method already implemented for small-set selection
subgroup bootstrapping gives an interval for AUROC scoring, improving precision by measuring stability given the low prevalence rate, compounded by splitting unbalanced subgroups, i.e. only 22 positive class females
subgroup testing now uses corrected resampled t-test (Nadeau & Bengio, 2003) to account for non-independence between cross-validation folds and repeats
calibration intercept fitted with the slope held at 1 (Van Calster et al., 2019), and the subgroup audit run on the final model’s own predictions
